lesson_title: The Coffee Bean's Journey: Why Raw Sellers Stay Poor
hook_text: A farmer earns a few rand for a kilogram of coffee beans. In Sandton, that kilogram sells for hundreds. Where did the money go?
clip_script: Imagine a street with one spaza shop and one giant supermarket. The spaza sells what it gathers cheaply — loose fruit, firewood. The supermarket sells processed goods, where the profit lives. And here is the trap: the spaza owner sells cheap raw things and buys expensive processed things, every single day. Money trickles one way. That street is the world economy. Countries selling ore and unroasted beans are the spaza; countries selling machines and medicines are the supermarket. Follow one coffee bean: the farmer gets a few rand per kilogram. Roasted, branded, and served in a Sandton cup, that kilogram earns hundreds — and the difference stays where the PROCESSING happens, not where the bean grew. It gets worse. Say one bag of oranges used to swap for one phone. Over the years, phone prices climb and orange prices sag, until the same phone costs three bags. You grow more, ship more, and afford less — through no fault of your own. Economists call that deteriorating terms of trade, and it is the quiet mechanism keeping raw-material countries running up an escalator that moves down. The escape? Stop selling only the beans and start selling the coffee. South Korea did exactly that — T-shirts to steel to ships to cars to computer chips in two generations. South Africa's car factories are our foot on that same ladder.
visual_style: A single animated coffee bean travelling from a Limpopo-style farm through a container ship, a roastery and a glossy café, with the price multiplying at each step; then orange bags stacking ever higher against one unchanging phone; closing on a ladder of products rising from T-shirt to microchip.
pacing: Quick market-scene open, deliberate slow build on the three-bags reveal, rapid triumphant ladder climb to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and follow the money through any trade route on earth.
